pro_tips: About two miles from the car, before the path climbs to Kangaroo Pass, leave it for the scree gully that angles back toward the notch just north of Half Moon; the North Ridge starts in that notch
Belay at the obvious ledges; running pitches together causes rope drag
Carry cord to replace old tat at the rappel stations
before.descent_text: Descend the route. From the summit, downclimb the easy but exposed top of the ridge to the first anchor and rappel back down the line of ascent, using the ledges on the crest and its west side as stations, until you are back in the notch north of the peak. Carry two ropes; the stations are a mix of old fixed pitons, bolts, slung horns and nuts, some parties have found no fixed anchors at all, and any tat left there should be inspected and backed up. From the notch, descend the loose scree gully carefully (keep the party close to limit rockfall), and at its foot rejoin the climbers' path and follow it back north to the hairpin pullout on the highway.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-September to early October, when the ridge is dry and cool and the larches around Libby Lake turn gold

July.reason: The gully and knife-edge are usually snow-free, but little shade on the burned trail makes midday very hot.

June.reason: Snow often lingers in the loose approach gully and on the north side of the ridge, and the upper forest roads may still hold snow.

August.reason: Dry rock throughout the traverse; heat on the exposed approach and late-summer wildfire smoke are the usual limits.

October.reason: Peak larch color early in the month, but snow flurries can coat the 5.7 step and the loose gully, so watch the forecast.

November.reason: Snow and ice on the knife-edge and gully, and the forest roads to the trailhead can become snowbound.

September.reason: Cooler, stable weather on the exposed class 4 crest, and the larches in the basin start turning late in the month.

pro_tips: Carry a short rope (~30 ft) if you'd rather protect or rappel the 5.7 overhang than free-solo it
Best done Raven Ridge to Hoodoo, as in the only documented trip report of this line

what_to_bring: Backpacking/camp gear for a 2-3 day trip (Ridge Lake or Gravel Lake camp)
Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass
Navigation aids for cross-country ridge travel
watch_out: A loose block on the downclimb into the notch could be dislodged onto PCT hikers on the trail far below — handle it with care.
Rappel anchors have been described as 'a bit dodgy' — inspect and back them up as needed.
The crumbly Class 2 traverse ledge crosses above a large cliff with real exposure.
pro_tips: A 60m rope is strongly recommended for the rappel off the summit block — a 40m rope is too short for one full rappel.
Most parties split the roughly 20+ mile round trip over 2-3 days, camping at Ridge Lake or Gravel Lake.
Technical approach or rock shoes help on the summit block even though most of the day is a trail/scramble approach.
before.approach: From the PCT North Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass (~3,000 ft), hike the PCT northbound via Kendall Pass and the Kendall Katwalk to Ridge Lake, then continue past Alaska Pass and around Joe Lake to the rolling meadows of Huckleberry Flats, roughly 10-11 miles one-way. Most parties camp at Ridge Lake, about 7 miles and 2,700 ft of gain from the trailhead. From Huckleberry Flats, leave the PCT and climb to the base of the east ridge at roughly 6,100 ft, where a rocky buttress marks the start of the technical ridge.

pro_tips: A 75-ft/23m rope is enough for the short belays/lowers on the Northwest Ridge, but rappelling the 100-ft summit gully in one go takes a 60m rope doubled — with the short rope, plan to downclimb the gully
Bring pickets specifically for the Ruth and Icy Glacier crossings, not just the ridge
Go early-to-mid summer, before the glaciers melt down to bare ice, as they have in some years
watch_out: The Ruth and Icy Glaciers can melt out to bare ice by mid-to-late summer, changing the character and difficulty of the route
Icy's Northwest Ridge to the Southeast (true) summit is steep, loose, and wildly exposed despite being 'only' 4th class
This is a long day — about 16 miles and 8,000 ft of cumulative gain/loss round trip

pro_tips: Most parties turn around at the west (false) summit where the register is kept -- if you want the true high point, continue to the east summit, which is 15-40 feet higher.
The trail junction partway to White Pass has a 'To Pilot Ridge' sign; stay straight/left through the valley rather than following it.
Doing this as an out-and-back from a Glacier Peak climb (via White Pass/Indian Pass) is a common way parties combine objectives on the same backpack.
watch_out: The final corkscrew move onto the southeast face to reach the true (east) summit is loose and exposed -- test holds carefully.
Lower slopes below the open scree/talus involve real bushwhacking through brush.
Indian Pass camp area has tent sites but no reliable water source nearby; plan water carries accordingly.
afternoon thunderstorms
loose rock
exposure on summit block
before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the ridge and the Class 2–3 gully back down to the North/South col, then pick your way back down the talus, slabs, and any lingering snow to Lake Ingalls, and rejoin Ingalls Way Trail #1390 back over Ingalls Pass to the Esmeralda Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble — no fixed rappel anchors exist on the standard South Peak route and the great majority of parties downclimb the entire route car-to-car in a day. Watch for loose rock and scree in the gully below the col (parties should stay bunched or descend one at a time to avoid knocking rock onto climbers below), and for the same lingering steep snow/ice near the col noted on the approach, which can make the downclimb more consequential than the ascent, especially early or late season. Some parties in icy conditions choose to sling a natural rock horn or block near the col and back up the short Class 3 step with a hand line or short rappel for extra security, but this is a personal-judgment call, not a standard part of the route, and no such anchor is left in place.

pro_tips: Approach in trail shoes to Home Lake and switch to rock shoes at the base of the buttress.
Study the face from Home Lake before starting — route-finding on this rotten, featureless rock is difficult once you're on it.

before.approach: Start at the Snowgrass Trailhead (elev. ~4,650 ft), reached via FR-21 (Johnson Creek Road) off US-12 about 3 miles west of Packwood. From the trailhead, follow the Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; the trail drops slightly (~75 ft) to cross Goat Creek on a footbridge/plank crossing around the 2-mile mark (only real water crossing on the approach, and a reliable water source — top off here or at the creeks in upper Snowgrass Flat). Continue climbing through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower Snowgrass Flat, then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft (about 4 miles / ~1,800 ft gain from the trailhead) — a broad, popular wildflower meadow, closed to camping, with multiple small creeks (last dependable water before the ridge). From Upper Snowgrass Flat, continue about 0.3–0.5 mile further to the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT north to about 6,700 ft, then leave it and head off-trail to the northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread (occasional cairns) toward the low col on the ridge crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak — expect loose, unconsolidated talus that shifts underfoot; test holds and footing carefully. From the col, follow the ridge crest or a line just south of it (Class 2) over a rounded intermediate high point toward Ives' northwest ridge. At the base of the true summit block, a boot path threads up scree toward a notch between two rock outcrops; above the notch is a short cliff band — downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge (Class 2) to gain the upper south face, then scramble roughly 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock and up easy terrain to the 7,920-ft summit. Snowfields commonly linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July (this basin can hold 25–40 ft of winter snowpack), so an ice axe is worth carrying for early/mid-season attempts on the traverse.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through mid-September, once the crest and shaded gullies have melted out and before fall storms move in

July.reason: Within the best-season window, but shaded NE slopes/gullies can still hold snow early in the month

June.reason: Deep lingering snow; the crest can still be in near-winter condition and route-finding is harder

August.reason: Peak of the best-season window; most consistently snow-free and stable conditions

October.reason: Outside the best-season window; early snow and storms can quickly turn this into full winter mountaineering

September.reason: Still within the best-season window; stable but a shorter weather window before fall storms

watch_out: Chossy, loose andesite on the Class 3 south face — test holds before weighting them
Exposed ledge/gap traverse below the summit notch
No bail-out shelter on the open crest if thunderstorms build
McCall Glacier moat/snow bridge near the Old Snowy-Ives col can be tricky in early-mid summer

before.approach: Access is from the south, through the Jerry Lakes basin. From the Canyon Creek Trailhead (~1,900 ft, SR 20 near MP 141), ford Canyon Creek and take the McMillan Park-Jackita Ridge Trail #738 to the Crater Mountain trail, continue past Crater Lake, then leave the trail between about 6,400 and 6,700 ft for a saddle at about 7,200 ft. From the saddle, cross the Jerry Glacier and drop into the Jerry Lakes basin, where nearly everyone camps; the route starts low on the glacier on the east side of the mountain, several hundred feet down into the next basin north. Most parties on Jack take three to four days for any route. No turn-by-turn approach exists for the East Ridge itself, so study satellite imagery before committing to a line.
what_to_bring: Headlamp and spare batteries - this is a long day
Map, compass and GPS with your intended approach line loaded
2-3 L water capacity plus a filter
Tent, bag and stove for 3-4 nights
ice axe and crampons — glacier approach
before.descent_text: The East Ridge is one of the mountain's more reasonable descents — at least one documented party climbed the North Ridge specifically so they could descend this ridge. Reversing it means downclimbing sustained Class 4 on loose rock with big exposure, so carry enough slings and cord to leave rappel anchors on blocks where downclimbing is unattractive. There are no fixed anchors. If you approached from the east glacier, the descent puts you back on the glacier and you should be roped for the crossing. The alternative — descending the South Face and exiting over Jerry Lakes — is a viable escape but leaves you a long way from an eastern or northern camp. Plan and scout the descent before you climb, and leave real daylight margin: the published figure of 9.5 hours from low on the glacier is for the ascent alone.

what_to_bring: Tent, sleeping bag and stove for 2-3 nights
Shell and insulating layers - the north cirque is cold and shaded
Headlamp and spare batteries (long pre-dawn starts and a real chance of finishing in the dark)
GPS with the bushwhack line recorded on the way up - navigating the timber at night is the crux of many trips
Sunglasses and full sun protection for the glacier
2-3 L water capacity and a stove to melt snow at a glacier camp
Gaiters and gear you do not mind soaking on the bushwhack
Skis or a splitboard if you want the descent as a bonus - the glacier has been skied
ice axe and technical tool — most parties climb with one axe plus one technical tool each; the winter ascent through the cliff band used one technical and one straight-shafted tool per climber
snowshoes or skis — approach and glacier; most parties use them

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: May, in a cold spell, while the headwall snow is continuous and the bergschrund is still bridged

May.reason: Long days, a still-bridged bergschrund and a continuous headwall; SR 20 usually opens mid-month, and a cold window keeps the 55-degree snow firm.

July.reason: The schrund is typically open, the lower glacier is broken up and the headwall snow is sun-rotted; this is not a summer route.

June.reason: The bergschrund opens quickly, often to a single bridge, and warm afternoons load the headwall with wet slides.

April.reason: Snowpack is continuous from about 4,800 ft and the schrund is closed, but the highway is usually still gated, adding a bike leg from MP 134.

March.reason: SR 20 is still gated at MP 134, so parties bike or ski in; winter slab and cornice hazard on the headwall is still high.

before.approach: No turn-by-turn approach is published. The north flank of Jack Mountain is reached from the Ross Lake East Bank Trail, which begins at the East Bank Trailhead on SR 20 near milepost 138 (~1,800 ft); Ross Lake Resort's water taxi will also drop parties at points along the eastern shore, which shortens the trail walking considerably. Devils Creek is the main north-side drainage and the East Bank Trail crosses it. From wherever you leave the trail, expect a steep, brushy, cliff-banded climb through timber to reach open ground and the base of the ridge — on the Nohokomeen side, the same belt of terrain has cliff bands starting around 3,200 ft, threaded on game trails to reach snow near 4,800-5,000 ft. Treat the approach as exploratory: study current imagery and plan the line before committing.
watch_out: Public beta is very thin - the 1971 first-ascent record and one modern trip report are close to the whole documented history.
Class 4 on loose greenstone with sustained exposure; a slip is unlikely to be arrested.
The approach through steep timber and cliff bands is the crux of the logistics and is genuinely hard to navigate in the dark.
Descending the East Ridge means committing to a second Class 4 route you have not climbed - scout it first.
The north side has no quick exit; an injury here is a multi-day evacuation.
pro_tips: Read the 2006 trip report (up the North Ridge, down the East Ridge) - it is the fullest modern account of this line and it establishes the traverse as the sensible plan.
Record a GPS track through the bushwhack on the way up. North-side parties on this mountain consistently report needing one to find their way back through the cliff bands after dark.
Consider the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to cut the East Bank Trail mileage; it is an established way onto this side of the mountain.
This was the mountain's first modern technical route (1971) and it still sees very little traffic - do not expect cairns, fixed gear or a boot track.
Carry axe and crampons even in August; the north aspect holds snow long after the south face has dried out.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September; October is a shoulder month as fall snow returns

July.reason: Trail and Katwalk are typically opening up, but early-month attempts can still find lingering steep snow on the Katwalk traverse

August.reason: Prime scramble season; trail and summit slopes typically fully melted out

October.reason: Good until snow returns; shortening daylight and increasing chance of early-season snow on the summit block

September.reason: Stable weather, fall colors, and lighter crowds than peak summer

what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass for trailhead parking
free self-issue wilderness permit (fill out at the trailhead)
map or GPS track — the boot path is unmarked and easy to lose
extra layers — the Katwalk and summit ridge are fully exposed to wind
ice axe — early season, snow on the PCT traverse and summit slopes
watch_out: the bleached stump landmark can be hard to spot in low light, fog, or if it has changed/fallen since older trip reports were written — carry a GPS track as backup
do not confuse the easier north-summit boot path with the harder Class 3-4 south ridge route to the other sub-summits
stay well back from the edge on the Katwalk itself, especially with kids or dogs — it has claimed a life

before.descent_text: Either reverse the ascent line, or descend north through a gully toward a rock feature known as The Smokestack, circle it clockwise to grassy ledges, descend the north ridge to the Klawatti Glacier, and follow glacier travel to the McAllister Glacier rappel station.
pro_tips: Camp near Klawatti Col to combine this with Austera Peak and/or Eldorado's other routes in one trip
before.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From camp, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) climbing the Eldorado Glacier to the high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration ice cap, typically another 3-5 hours. Any overnight stay requires a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Important — this route is not on Eldorado Peak itself: from the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600ft), continue traversing the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti col; Tepeh Towers are passed along this same glacier traverse, and Austera Peak requires further travel across the Klawatti Glacier (including a short rappel from the col) beyond Klawatti Peak — meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado.

The standard approach follows the North Fork Sauk River Trail (USFS Trail #649) from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (~2,050 ft), reached via Forest Road 49 off the Mountain Loop Highway south of Darrington. The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the river valley for about 5.5 miles to Mackinaw Shelter — a possible camp, though tight for a larger party — crossing several tributaries en route, including Red Creek, which parties describe as interesting but not difficult to ford in normal flow (a trekking pole/sturdy stick helps with balance); it can run considerably higher during spring snowmelt or after rain. Past the shelter the trail turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks through subalpine forest to a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail in a meadow (~6,000 ft) with the first real views of Glacier Peak and the White Chuck/Kololo massif. Turn right (north) on the PCT and follow it about a quarter mile to White Pass (5,900 ft) — roughly 9 miles and 4,800+ ft of gain from the trailhead, and the last reliable, easy water source before the high traverse. From White Pass the maintained trail ends and the route becomes a boot path: traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin / White River Meadows (~6,300-6,500 ft), the common base camp, either via Red Pass (1.2 miles from the PCT junction) or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck River basin (the 'Foam Pass' variant). From camp, climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier and Glacier Gap onto the White River Glacier — this is glacier travel, and rope/crampons/axe are standard gear here; crevasses are typically open and visible to weave around by late summer but can be harder to read under early-season snow bridges. From the gap, drop a short way onto the White River Glacier and come at the peak from the south, climbing the snow headwall to the summit ridge and an easy talus-and-ledge scramble to the summit (Class 2+). This is a long approach in its own right — the round trip runs roughly 28-30 miles — so almost all parties camp at White River Meadows or Foam Basin rather than attempting the trailhead-to-summit push in a single push. There are two long approaches: this North Fork Sauk line, and the alternate White River Trail approach from the east, which reaches a similar high basin by a comparably long trail-plus-cross-country line.

pro_tips: Go when avalanche danger is low and the couloir is filled with firm snow/ice
Other Lane Peak couloirs (e.g., The Fly) offer similar climbs
watch_out: avalanche
cornices
brittle/variable ice
what_to_bring: ice axe — one per climber, 50cm+ technical or straight-shaft aluminum

watch_out: The summit block has a cliff band on its north side — don't wander north off the ridge/face line, especially in fog.
Snow/ice can linger in the summit gully into August in heavier-snow years — carry an ice axe even in mid-summer.
The gap-to-lakes boot path along La Bohn Creek is unmaintained, steep, and easy to lose — note your route for the return.
pro_tips: Base-camp at La Bohn Lakes or upper Necklace Valley and day-trip the summit — it's a quick, worthwhile add-on from the gap.
Pair with Mount Hinman (1.7 mi east) for a two-summit day if conditions and daylight allow.
Filter water at La Bohn Lakes; carry what you need for the final scramble, which is dry.

before.approach: Start at White River Campground (4,400 ft) off WA-410 (the driving approach is covered separately). Follow the Glacier Basin Trail up the White River valley about 3.5 miles, gaining roughly 1,500 ft, crossing the West Fork White River on a footbridge, to Glacier Basin camp (~5,900 ft) beneath the Inter Glacier — this is the last dependable running water before the route goes onto snow and ice for good. From Glacier Basin the maintained trail ends; leave it and climb snow/scree slopes east toward St. Elmo Pass (~7,400 ft), a boot-track/climber's route (not signed or maintained) between Mt. Ruth and the Inter Glacier that can be icy in early season and can develop cornices. From St. Elmo Pass, drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and contour counter-clockwise (roped glacier travel with crevasse-rescue gear required from here on) beneath Mt. Ruth, crossing the Winthrop and traversing under/around Curtis Ridge to a ramp that accesses the Carbon Glacier at about 7,300 ft — there are established bivy sites in this access gully. This traverse sits below Willis Wall and Ptarmigan Ridge, so icefall and rockfall (worsening as the day warms) are real hazards; parties typically move through early. From the Carbon Glacier access, ascend the glacier as directly as crevasses allow to the base of Liberty Ridge, climb a snow ramp onto the ridge crest from its east side, cross to the west side, and continue up snow slopes and rock outcrops to Thumb Rock (10,775 ft), the standard high camp — flat, wind-sheltered tent sites but no liquid water (melt snow/ice). White River to Thumb Rock is commonly a long single push (7-10+ hours) or split with the Curtis Ridge bivy; expect sustained roped glacier travel, crevasse hazard on the Winthrop and Carbon crossings, and rockfall/icefall exposure under Willis Wall. Above Thumb Rock the ridge steepens through sustained ice runnels past the Black Pyramid rock band before the final steep ice leads onto the upper mountain near Liberty Cap; rockfall/serac hazard grows as the day warms, so climb this section early.

watch_out: Liberty Wall serac calving is the route's primary objective hazard and looms directly over sections of the climb.
Crux chimney conditions are highly variable — confirm current ice coverage before attempting.
The approach glaciers (Mowich/upper Carbon) carry significant crevasse hazard requiring careful route-finding.
pro_tips: The crux chimney climbs completely differently depending on conditions — ice-filled it's a WI3 pitch, bare it's insecure 5.6 rock in mountaineering boots and crampons, so check recent trip reports before committing.
Liberty Wall's serac directly overhangs part of the route — move through the most exposed sections early and quickly.
Carry a light rock rack in addition to screws and pickets since ice coverage on the crux varies year to year.

watch_out: loose footing on upper talus
before.approach: Park at the Smithbrook Trailhead (elev. ~4,000 ft) on Smithbrook Road (FR 6700), about 3 miles up from Hwy 2. Start on the signed Smithbrook Trail (part of the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness trail system) and climb via nearly 20 short switchbacks, gaining about 650 ft in about a mile to Union Gap on the PCT — Lichtenberg's summit is visible to the south for much of this stretch once the forest opens up. At Union Gap, turn left (south) onto the Pacific Crest Trail and follow it about 2 miles, contouring below Lichtenberg's east flank, to Lake Valhalla (~4,830 ft), passing through a mix of forest and open meadow/heather and crossing Smith Brook along the way (a reliable water source and a good place to filter before leaving the trail). From the north or east shore of Lake Valhalla, leave the PCT and begin the off-trail portion: contour and rising-traverse around the lake toward the peak's south/southwest side, picking through heather benches, boulder fields, and increasingly loose talus. There is no maintained trail above the lake — expect real route-finding, some bushwhacking through scattered subalpine fir, and a few short cliff bands that force minor backtracking; a GPS track or written beta is genuinely useful here. The standard line aims for a prominent gully on the south/southwest side of the summit tower (often snow-filled into early summer — an ice axe and sometimes light traction are worth carrying outside of peak summer), climbed as scree/talus with a bit of low third-class scrambling near the top to gain the final summit block. Total gain from the trailhead is roughly 2,000-2,500 ft over about 9 miles round trip, with 6-7 hours being a typical leisurely round-trip time.

pro_tips: The road walk is the crux of the winter day, not the mountain. It is usually packed hard by other parties, so boots often work as well as snowshoes for the first 2 miles.

Load the compass bearings, not just a track: 177 degrees true from the road to Lichtenwasser Lake and 248 degrees from the lake's south end to the 5,640-foot saddle. The forested lower section is featureless in flat light.
Cross Lichtenwasser Lake directly if it is solidly frozen — it saves a slow traverse around the shore. Verify the ice first.
The north side generally holds better snow quality through the winter than the south, which is the main reason to prefer this line over the Yodelin approach.
In summer, camping at Lichtenwasser Lake makes this a relaxed overnight and lets you tag The Lichtenhorn as well as the main summit, which is what the 1975 party did.
If you want a circuit, climbing this side and descending south toward Yodelin works — but the south exit crosses private ground near the lodge, so ask permission before you leave a car there.
This route reaches the true 5,844-foot summit; the west peak (The Lichtenhorn, ~5,800 ft) is a separate top requiring a further scramble west along the ridge.

what_to_bring: crampons — rigid front points suitable for 70-80 degree ice
two ice axes — one for climbing, one for safety

watch_out: numerous false summits/points along the ridge before the true summit — a commonly reported frustration on the approach
cross-country ledge and ridge sections above Butte Pass/Shellrock Pass have no cairns or trail
loose talus and scree on the south/southwest slopes — the Butte Pass line avoids the worst of it
what_to_bring: free self-issue wilderness permit (fill out at the trailhead register)
topo map + compass or GPS/inReach — much of the route is cross-country with no trail
layers for wind-exposed, cold ridges even in July/August

watch_out: Significant side-hilling through the basins causes foot fatigue over a multi-day trip
The class 3+ traverse on the north side beneath the summit is exposed
pro_tips: The connecting route between Boulder, Clark, and Luahna basins is a faint, unmaintained sheepherder's trail — expect real routefinding and significant side-hilling that is hard on the feet

watch_out: The false-summit-to-true-summit traverse looks intimidating from a distance but is only Class 3–4 on solid rock — most parties do it unroped; needing a rope here is generally a sign to turn around, not to push on
Devil's club and slide alder in the Access Creek brush hide slick logs and holes — expect slow going and consider gaiters/long sleeves
Big Beaver and Access Creek fords are cold and can run thigh-to-waist deep even in August after a warm spell
Cairns are sparse across the cross-country basins between Access Col and Luna Pass; a whiteout here makes route-finding genuinely difficult

before.descent_text: Rappel from the installed bolts on the ridge or downclimb the same broken rock and slabs to the saddle between Lundin Peak and East Lundin Peak. From the saddle, follow the climbers' path over to Red Pass, then take the Commonwealth Creek trail down to the PCT and out to the parking lot at the Snoqualmie Pass exit. Allow about two hours from East Lundin to the car. The three large bolts are best treated as landmarks and a rappel anchor to back up.

Most parties reverse the West Ridge: from the true (west) summit, downclimb the class 3-4 ridge crest back toward the notch/saddle used on the way up, staying on the north side of the crest per the standard line and reversing the short crux step (a ~6 ft downclimb at a minor notch). Many parties downclimb this cleanly, but a single short rappel (roughly 15 m/50 ft, well within a 30 m single-rope length) is commonly used here instead, especially in wet conditions or with less experienced climbers — anchors are natural (slung horns/blocks or a small nut/cam placement backed by a cordelette), not bolted; there's no fixed hardware on this route. From the saddle, either reverse the ascent couloir into Lundin Basin (a fast glissade of up to 1,200-1,500 ft when it's still snow-filled, typically only reliable early season) or walk scree/talus down toward the Red-Lundin col to pick up the use trail back into Commonwealth Basin and the PCT. An alternative some parties use is descending the East Ridge instead: scramble down the crest about 100 ft to the top of a small cliff band, then make one single-rope rappel (30 m is sufficient; natural tree/horn anchors — the ridge has plenty of trees to sling) down to easy ledges, continuing to a notch in the ridge crest from which an early-season glissade or scramble rejoins the standard route in Lundin/Commonwealth Basin. This option requires either looping back on foot into Commonwealth Basin or a car shuttle/hitch between the Alpental and PCT-North trailheads, since the two approaches start at different lots. Bottom line for planning: expect zero to one short rappel (under 15 m, single rope, natural gear anchors — no bolts) — conditions and party comfort level determine whether it's downclimbed or rapped. Total descent to the trailhead runs roughly 2-2.5 hours.

watch_out: The climber's path from Cascade Pass toward Cache Col is unmaintained and easy to lose in poor visibility — many parties end up traversing too high or low on Mixup Peak's east slopes
The false summit is roughly 300 ft SE of, and lower than, the true high point — don't stop there
pro_tips: Many parties combine Magic Mountain with the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse or nearby Spider-Formidable objectives, basing out of Kool-Aid Lake
Snow conditions on the Cache Glacier/Cache Col crossing change quickly through the season — check recent trip reports before deciding on ice axe vs. crampons

The final miles of Cascade River Road are rough gravel and frequently washout-damaged; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended, and it's worth checking the NPS road-conditions page the day before you drive
before.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,660 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), follow the Cascade Pass Trail — a well-graded, heavily switchbacked National Park trail — 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft of gain to Cascade Pass (5,360-5,400 ft), the low notch between Mixup Peak and Cascade Peak. This section is on-trail, well-marked, and passable by early-to-mid summer once the switchbacks melt out; it's also the most crowded stretch since it's a popular day hike in its own right. At the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up a climber's path bearing south-southeast, making a rising traverse across open heather and snow benches on the east flank of Mixup Peak. This climber's trail is intermittent and route-finding becomes more important in early season when it's snow-covered. Continue the traverse to the base of the Cache Glacier (~6,000 ft), then ascend moderate snow slopes (up to about 35 degrees) to Cache Col (6,900-6,960 ft); the glacier here is small and generally reported free of significant crevasse hazard, but an ice axe and sometimes crampons are worth carrying for the snow slope depending on season and firmness. From Cache Col, descend roughly 600 ft on a climber's path with a descending traverse to the southeast, dropping to Kool-Aid Lake (about 6,120 ft), the standard camp/bivy area for Magic Mountain and the broader Ptarmigan Traverse. From Kool-Aid Lake, the final approach climbs about 1,000 ft directly up heather and scree slopes to the col (~7,100 ft) separating Magic Mountain from neighboring Hurry Up Peak, which is where the South Ridge proper begins. There is reliable water at Kool-Aid Lake and seasonal snowmelt along the traverse, but none on the upper ridge itself. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at the trailhead and a backcountry camping permit is required from North Cascades National Park for overnight stays at Kool-Aid Lake; most parties treat this as a 2-day trip with a camp at the lake rather than a car-to-car push given the off-trail navigation.

watch_out: The summit pyramid's gully/rib network is genuinely confusing — several parties have gotten cliffed out; carry route photos or a GPX track rather than relying on the general description.

before.descent_text: Standard descent is to reverse the ascent line: follow the exposed ridge crest back to the top of the west gully, downclimb the gully (steep Class 3/4 at its base) to Mesahchie Col, then reverse the slabs and the crest of the shoulder between Mesahchie and Katsuk down to the basin below the col. From camp, retrace the sidehill traverse, crossing the waterfall on the same bench near 6,500 ft, back to Easy Pass, and descend the trail to the trailhead. There is no mandatory rappelling - this is a Class 3-4 scramble route and parties downclimb the entire way. Loose talus, scree and gully rock throughout are the main hazards on the way down; keep the party out from under each other in the gully.

before.descent_text: Most parties descend the route itself, back down the North Ridge toward high camp; it is non-technical, mostly Class 2 over loose volcanic scree. before.approach: Killen Creek Trailhead (Trail #113, off FR 2329 via FR 23) climbs through forest and meadow ~3.1 mi/1,400 ft to the PCT, then continues to High Camp — roughly 4 mi and 2,300 ft of gain total from the trailhead — the shared base camp for the North Ridge, Adams Glacier, and Northwest Ridge routes.

pro_tips: Ascend via the steep Switchback Trail and descend via Klahhane Ridge/High Ridge Trail (or vice versa) to make a loop and see more terrain for a similar overall distance.

before.approach: Primary approach: drive the narrow, one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road (Olympic NP's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft; usually open only early/mid-July through mid-October) 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass, then continue on the Cameron Pass Trail about 3.5 more miles, climbing to Cameron Pass (~6,450-6,500 ft) and the camp sites in the basin below it (roughly 9-10 miles one-way to a base camp, off-trail beyond that to the summit ridge). Alternative southern approach: from Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking, some 8.5 miles from US-101, forcing a long walk/bike up the old roadbed before even reaching the Dosewallips River Trail proper and then the multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin — this route adds many extra miles and is rarely used as the primary option today.
before.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line back down to the Cameron Basin/Cameron Pass camp, then retrace the Cameron Pass Trail and Grand Pass Trail back to the Obstruction Point trailhead (or continue the much longer exit down the Dosewallips if that was the approach used). No rope work or rappels are typical on the standard scramble; the main descent hazards are loose scree/talus on the upper slopes and, early in the season, glissading or downclimbing residual snowfields on north-facing terrain.

watch_out: The Catwalk is the crux of the climb—treat it with respect and expect high exposure.
Helmet is mandatory; rockfall is frequent from loose, unstable rock.
Before mid-July, expect deep snow on the Catwalk; ice axe and crampons required.
Wildlife encounter risk; black bears present in the area.

before.approach: There is no established route to Mount Carrie from Hurricane Ridge; that area is separated from the Bailey Range by miles of trailless, glaciated terrain and functions only as a viewpoint. The actual approach used by essentially all climbers starts at the Sol Duc River Road trailhead (~2,000 ft) on US-101 near Lake Crescent: Sol Duc Falls → Deer Lake Trail junction (+1 mi) → Heart Lake (+7 mi, 4,800 ft) → High Divide crest (+0.5 mi, 5,100 ft) → east on the Cat Basin trail toward Cat Basin → an unmaintained path over Cat Peak's exposed south side and across the airy "Catwalk" ridge (Class 3) to Boston Charlie's Camp. From camp, the final push follows Carrie's southwest ridge (Class 1 grass/rock) and contours a broad, steep, loose south-facing scree basin around 6,500 ft before a scree-and-snow finish (ice axe advisable) to the summit (Class 2). One-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is roughly 13 miles.
before.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line. From the summit, descend the southwest ridge and the south-facing scree basin below it to Boston Charlie's Camp, keeping the helmet on - the rock here is loose and rockfall is the reason the helmet is mandatory on this route - and carrying the axe for any steep snow still lying in the basin early in the season. From Boston Charlie's, re-cross the Catwalk to Cat Peak. This is the crux of the day in descent exactly as it is in ascent: a narrow rock and heather ridge with substantial exposure where a fall could be fatal, and descending a scramble is generally the more hazardous direction, so cross it in daylight and with full attention rather than hurrying it at the end of a long day. From Cat Peak follow the High Divide back to Heart Lake, then take the Sol Duc River Trail out to the trailhead. There is no rappelling anywhere on the standard line.

before.approach: From the Obstruction Point Trailhead (6,150 ft), reached by the narrow, unpaved Obstruction Point Road that leaves Hurricane Ridge Road just below Hurricane Ridge, follow the Grand Pass Trail along open Lillian Ridge, then down into Grand Valley past Grand and Moose Lakes and up past Gladys Lake to Grand Pass (6,488 ft) at about 6 miles. Net gain to the pass is only a few hundred feet, but the trail first loses well over 1,000 ft into the valley, so total climbing to the pass is close to 2,000 ft. Beyond Grand Pass the trail drops steeply into Cameron Basin, then climbs steeply to Cameron Pass (6,448 ft), the highest trail-served pass in the park; the last part of that climb is loose and rocky in spots and holds snow into midsummer. From Cameron Pass the primitive trail descends into Lost Basin at the head of the Lost River and continues to Lost Pass (5,570 ft), the low notch between Lost Peak and Claywood. Parties camp in Upper Cameron Basin or in Lost Basin and climb the peak from there. At Lost Pass leave the trail and head west-southwest across open heather benches and talus toward Claywood, the higher, greyer and more broken summit about a mile and a half away. The final several hundred feet are class 2-3 scrambling on broken shale and loose scree, with a short class 3 step on the west side of the summit block. Everything beyond Lost Pass is unmarked and off-trail, so carry a map and GPS and go only in good visibility.

before.approach: From the Upper Dungeness/Royal Basin Trailhead (elev. ~2,500 ft), hike the Upper Dungeness River Trail roughly 7 miles with about 2,500 ft of gain to Royal Lake, then continue about a mile farther into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600 ft), a meadow-and-tarn basin ringed by Deception, Mystery, Fricaba, and Hal Foss Peak. From the upper basin, leave the trail and head southwest over the moraine to the big snow slope on the west edge of the northeast face. Climb it most of the way toward the low point of the Deception-Martin ridge, then break left into the steep side gully that gives the route its name; from its top, traverse left and climb a second snow-and-rock gully to the summit ridge. Allow roughly 3 hours from the upper basin to the top of the gully in good snow. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed at the trailhead and a wilderness permit is required for overnight stays.

Start at the Upper Trailhead (about 3,500 ft) at the end of the spur off FS 24, which needs a Northwest Forest Pass. Trail 812 climbs at once, with stacked switchbacks for the first 0.3 mile before it merges with the lower-trailhead trail near 3,900 ft. Continue up through forest to the signed junction near timberline, about 4,500 ft, where the winter climbers' route leaves the summer trail and goes right. Follow the heavily used footpath along the north fork of Big Creek into the basin below the south-face chute, which is the base of the climb and a usual place for a first break.

There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. At 0.8 mi pass Sol Duc Falls, and at 0.9 mi reach the Lovers Lane junction; branch left onto the Deer Lake Trail, which climbs steeply and relentlessly through switchbacks to Deer Lake (3.4 mi, ~3,527 ft) — the first reliable water and the last easy camping before things get serious. Beyond Deer Lake the trail continues up through Potholes Meadows (~5 mi) and gains the High Divide ridge crest around 6 mi/4,730 ft, with good views and intermittent tarns/snowmelt for water. At 7.4 mi pass the Seven Lakes Basin junction (4,900 ft) — a good last water/camp option — then continue along High Divide past or near Bogachiel Peak (5,474 ft). At roughly 10.2 mi, leave the maintained trail system at the Cat Basin junction; from here it is off-trail cross-country and boot-path travel only, dropping into Cat Basin below Cat Peak (5,940 ft) and then crossing the Catwalk, the narrow, exposed class 3 ridge linking Cat Peak to Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). Past it, many parties use the exposed, loose-talus sidehill traverse across Carrie's south face; an alternative preferred by some climbers is to stay higher on Carrie's north side, which avoids the worst sidehilling and leads up Carrie's ridge and upper flanks to its summit. The route to Fairchild starts from Mount Carrie's summit: head northeast down the Carrie Glacier (rope up and put on crampons here; ice axe mandatory most of the season), circle around to the north of Fairchild, and climb its Southwest Ridge to the 6,899 ft summit. This final section is only thinly described, so expect to find the line yourself. One-way distance to this point is roughly 12 miles with substantial cumulative gain from repeated up-and-down over Bogachiel Peak, Cat Peak, and the Carrie ridge system, consistent with the ~8,000 ft round-trip gain. Hazards: early-season creek crossings near Sol Duc Falls, steep loose-scree switchbacks on the Deer Lake Trail, serious exposure and loose rock on the Catwalk traverse, crevasses and snow bridges on the Carrie Glacier requiring roped glacier travel (especially early/mid-summer), no reliable water between Cat Basin and the glacier, and heavy route-finding demands in fog/whiteout since the entire Cat Basin-to-summit section is unmarked wilderness travel.

before.descent_text: Descend the same way you came up: reverse the scree/talus ridge line down to the Fricaba–Hal Foss col, drop back into Deception Basin, climb back over Constance Pass, and descend to Home Lake (or continue the full ~9.6 miles out to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead if pushing it car-to-car in a day — most parties instead camp at Home Lake or in Deception Basin and hike out the next day). This is a non-technical walk-off/downclimb — Fricaba is consistently described as a fairly easy scramble and a scree walkup on shattered, rotten shale, and no fixed rappel anchors or technical rappel stations are reported on the North or SW ridge lines (unlike neighboring Mount Constance, which has a rap station off its summit). The main descent hazards are loose rock and ankle-turning scree underfoot in the rotten Fricaba rock, brief exposed Class 3 downclimbing moves near the ridge crest/col, and — in early season — glissading or firm snow on the Constance Pass/Deception Basin traverse, where an ice axe is recommended into early summer.

Start from a high camp to keep summit day manageable.

Excellent scrambling skills and comfort with exposure are essential

before.approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, start on Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 through second-growth and then old-growth forest along the Dungeness River. At about 1 mile, bear right at the signed junction onto the Royal Basin Trail (the left fork continues up-valley toward Boulder Shelter/Constance Pass). The Royal Basin trail then climbs gradually for several miles alongside Royal Creek — the main water source for the approach — crossing it on log/plank bridges more than once; these crossings can run fast and cold during early-season snowmelt (June). Around mile 6 the grade steepens sharply for the push to Royal Lake (7.2 mi, roughly 2,500 ft gained from the trailhead), with the final mile gaining about 500 ft on looser, sometimes-eroded tread. From Royal Lake continue south up-valley on the scramblers'/climbers' path roughly another 0.8 mile and 600 ft to Upper Royal Basin (about 8 mi in, ~5,700 ft), a broad heather-and-tarn basin below Mount Deception's northeast face that most parties use as base camp (NPS wilderness permit and bear canister required; no fires; advance reservations cover June 15–Oct 15). From Upper Royal Basin the maintained trail ends; head cross-country west up heather benches and talus to the rim of the glacial moraine ringing Surprise Basin, the small hanging cirque between Mount Martin, Mount Johnson, and Mount Clark. Drop into Surprise Basin and cross its snowfields (crampons/axe often useful into July) toward the roughly 6,900 ft notch/col between Johnson (climber's left) and Clark (climber's right) — this is the standard gateway to Johnson's upper mountain. This off-trail stretch above Upper Royal Basin is loose talus and scree with genuine rockfall and route-finding hazard; helmets on from the moraine rim upward. Given the total distance (~19 miles / 30.9 km round trip) and elevation gain, most parties backpack in and camp at Upper Royal Basin, climbing Johnson as a long day from camp rather than attempting it car-to-car.

before.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb from the summit back to the ~6,900 ft Johnson–Clark notch, then retrace the talus-and-moraine descent down into Surprise Basin and back over its rim to Upper Royal Basin, from which the Royal Basin/Upper Dungeness Trail leads back out to the trailhead. The summit chimney is downclimbed rather than rappelled; there are no fixed/bolted rappel stations reported on Johnson, so a party that wants a rope on the steepest step, particularly if the rock is wet, must rig it from a natural anchor (horn, chockstone, or slung block) of its own.

before.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling. Reverse the ridge and talus scramble back down to LaCrosse Pass, picking your way carefully back through the loose Class 2–3 terrain (descending loose talus is where most of the slip-and-slide hazard on this route actually lives, more than on the ascent). From the pass, descend the LaCrosse Pass Trail to whichever trailhead your itinerary uses. If you're headed out the Duckabush side, be ready for a knee-punishing, steep, switchbacking drop of about 3,000 ft in roughly a mile back to the Duckabush River Trail junction — this section is loose underfoot and eroded in spots, and is meaningfully harder on tired legs descending than it is climbing. If you're exiting north toward the Dosewallips/West Fork Dosewallips, the grade down from the pass is gentler and more forgiving. In poor visibility, the open, sparsely-cairned country right around the pass and upper basin is the spot most likely to cause route-finding trouble on the way down — many parties mention losing the tread in lingering snowfields near the pass well into early summer.

When SR 20 is closed at Easy Pass, the longer Thunder Creek way in (about 13 miles) starts at Colonial Creek Campground.

before.approach: Start at Easy Pass Trailhead at Highway 20 mile 151 (elevation 3,700 ft). Hike 3.5 miles gaining 2,800 feet to Easy Pass (6,500 ft). Descend into Fisher Basin via steep scenic trail through alpine meadows and forest (1.5 miles). Continue to Fisher Creek valley floor and established campsites. From camp area, cross Fisher Creek via large fallen log and travel east side of Douglas Creek valley on faint climber's path. This transition from forest to open terrain is where the route becomes extremely challenging—travelers encounter a vast field of slide alder and other brush, 10+ feet high, virtually impenetrable in many directions, with small rocky stream channels crisscrossing the ground. Progress is measured in inches per minute. Off-trail navigational skill critical.
before.descent_text: Descend the Banded Glacier via the Banded-Douglas col to reach the Fisher Creek basin, or reverse the Douglas Glacier with care back toward Easy Pass.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through August - enough snow remains on the snow finger and the glaciers before late-season bare, more crevassed ice

July.reason: Early July often still holds significant lingering snow; conditions improve toward late month

August.reason: Most reliable window: settled weather while the snow finger still holds snow, though the glaciers open up late in the month

September.reason: Still viable and often clear, but shortening daylight and increasing chance of early fall storms

before.approach: Long approach into the Entiat Mountains, via one of two options: from the Phelps Creek Trailhead, hike ~3.5 miles to the Leroy Creek crossing, then continue cross-country up to Leroy Basin and over the Seven Fingered Jack-Maude col; or drive Entiat River Road (becomes FR 51/5100) ~38 miles from Entiat to Cottonwood Campground, then hike the Entiat River Trail ~14.5 miles to the cirque below Maude, Seven Fingered Jack, and Fernow (this trail passes through terrain burned in the 2015 Wolverine Fire).

No maintained trail reaches the peak. Most parties approach via the Elwha River Trail from Whiskey Bend and over Dodwell-Rixon Pass into the Bailey Range highline route, or via the North Fork Quinault River Trail from the North Fork Quinault trailhead (not Graves Creek, which serves the East Fork and Enchanted Valley) to Low Divide, then up through Seattle Basin to the saddle just east of Mount Noyes. Either approach involves 3-5+ days of off-trail travel, river fords, and remote high camps before reaching the Noyes-Meany col.

The exposed 4th-class notch/step (~7,500 ft) can be wet, mossy, or icy early in the season
Don't confuse the route with Mount Deception (7,788 ft, immediately NNW) - the two peaks share the Royal/Deception Basin approach

pro_tips: Check current Hampton Resources (formerly Weyerhaeuser) gate/permit status before driving in — FR-62 access at Highway 2 changes without notice and is frequently locked.
Avoid the southwest approach from the head of Proctor Creek; its brush is thicker than the bristles of a paint brush.
The short mileage is misleading — budget 4.5+ hours car-to-car given the steepness and route-finding.
Treat Bathtub Lakes as a worthwhile standalone objective if you don't want to commit to the full scramble to the summit.
Go in late summer/fall for the best combination of dry rock and blueberry/fall-color scenery in the basin.
before.approach: From the Verlot Public Service Center on the Mountain Loop Highway, continue east about 4.6 miles and turn right onto Forest Road 4020 (Schweitzer Creek Road, signed for Boardman Lake/Ashland Lakes/Bear-Pinnacle Lake). Follow FR 4020 for 2.7 miles to a junction, take the right fork onto FR 4021, and continue 1.4 miles on a rough road to the Pinnacle Lake Trailhead (about 2,700 ft; small ~15-car lot, no toilet). Hike the Pinnacle Lake Trail to the lake, walk around its southwest shore to Iodine Creek, and follow the creek up through Iodine Gulch to its top; turn right and continue a short distance to the Bathtub Lakes basin. From there, continue scrambling west to reach Mount Pilchuck's summit.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: June to mid-July, while snow still bridges the creek valley and the glacier's crevasses before they open up

May.reason: Firm snow runs from the road-end clearcut to the glacier, but spring avalanche cycles off the Hanging Glacier and basin slopes are still active.

July.reason: Snow recedes from the valley bottom and the clearcut contour gets brushier, but crevasses on the White Salmon are usually still bridged early in the month.

June.reason: Deep snow still fills the creek valley and bridges most crevasses, so the approach avoids slide alder; cross under the Hanging Glacier early.

August.reason: The approach becomes a brushy contour with stream crossings, and crevasses on the White Salmon and Curtis glaciers open, lengthening route-finding.

October.reason: Shortening days, first autumn snow over open crevasses, and wet brush on the approach make this a poor time for the glacier.

September.reason: Bare, broken glacier and open crevasses make travel slow and circuitous, and the summit pyramid scramble is looser once snow is gone.

pro_tips: This is probably the most common descent route for northside Shuksan climbs, so know it even if climbing something else.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-summer through early fall (roughly late July into September) once the glacier is well-covered and consolidated but not yet icy

July.reason: Glacier bridges can still be present and route generally passable, but early-month snow can be less consolidated and afternoon thunderstorms are common

August.reason: Typically the most stable window - glacier well-consolidated, crevasses visible enough to navigate, and firm snow for cramponing on the summit approach

September.reason: Crevasses more open and visible as melt-out progresses (easier to see, less to step over blindly), but glacier ice is more exposed and early-season snowfall risk rises toward month's end

watch_out: The lower Depot Creek trail has been reported significantly degraded by logging and storm blowdown — expect bushwhacking, not a maintained tread
The Depot Creek Falls crossing gets climbers thoroughly soaked; hypothermia risk on a cold morning
The southwest glacier's crevasse/snow-bridge crossing is the technical crux — assess it fresh, not late in the day

before.approach: From the Depot Creek Road washout (~2,600 ft, reached via a rough 4WD spur off Chilliwack Lake Road out of Chilliwack Lake Provincial Park, BC), the hike-in starts on the old roadbed: walk it about 9 minutes to an inconspicuous spur road on the left, follow that spur roughly 4 minutes to a T-junction, then bear right onto an extremely overgrown, sporadically muddy road for about 35 minutes to Monument 65 at the US-Canada border (roughly 45 minutes/0.8 hr total from the washout). From the border the route becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path following Depot Creek through beautiful old-growth forest - easy going where deadfall has been cut out, though dozens of uncut logs remain to step over in places. About 3 miles in, the path reaches Depot Creek Falls, the approach's real crux: crossing wet, slick boulders and slabs at the base of the falls. An old fixed hand-line was still serviceable as of a 2017 NPS trip report and assists at the vertical step here, but it should be treated with caution and backed up if in doubt - this is the approach's primary hazard, especially with a pack on wet rock. Above the falls the path continues through Depot Creek Meadow and Upper Depot Creek to Ouzel (Silver) Lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat, sandy, mostly treeless benches that serve as the standard base camp for both Spickard and neighboring Mount Redoubt, about 5-6 miles and roughly 6 hours of hiking from the road-end washout; Depot Creek and Ouzel Lake itself provide reliable water throughout. From camp, gain the climbing route by ascending a broad talus couloir and stream drainage north/northeast toward the ~7,200 ft Silver Lake saddle; well before the actual pass, cut right around the toe of a steep rocky buttress into open heather-and-moraine basins and traverse to the toe of the Southwest Glacier, roughly 2.5 hours above camp. Rope up and don crampons/crevasse gear here: the glacier's climber's-right margin offers a line of hard 30-40 degree snow/ice with relatively few crevasses, but roughly halfway up, one distinctly 'inhospitable-looking' crevasse must be crossed on a marginal snowbridge - probe it carefully and be prepared for the bridge to have deteriorated depending on the season. A short, steep, loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on the ~8,000 ft col on Spickard's southwest ridge, the start of the summit scramble (easy 3rd-class rock and up to ~35-40 degree snow to the summit ridge).

From the Staircase trailhead area on the North Fork Skokomish River, follow the North Fork Skokomish River Trail 12.7 miles to First Divide (elevation about 4,688 ft), passing through lowland and montane forest into subalpine meadow with views of the La Crosse Peaks. From First Divide, continue cross-country to reach Mount Steel's summit.
watch_out: The 20+ km figure above covers only the trail to First Divide; the final push to the true summit is undocumented cross-country terrain, so budget extra time for route-finding.

pro_tips: The Kamikaze Trail reportedly gains about 2,300 ft in roughly a mile — treat it as a serious workout, not a casual variation.
Ascending Kamikaze and descending the standard trail via Rachor Pass makes a popular ~10-mile loop that avoids downclimbing the steepest, wettest sections.
Microspikes help through the cedar-grove shelf (~4,200 ft) where snow can linger into early summer.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July and September, when the steep Kamikaze rock steps are dry and snow-free and the south-facing slope is not at peak heat

May.reason: The lower boot track melts out, but patchy snow near the crest and wet, mossy rock steps make the Class 2-3 moves much harder than on the standard trail.

July.reason: Dry, grippy rock steps and firm tread on the steep boot track, with long days that suit the Kamikaze-up, standard-trail-down loop.

June.reason: The ridge crest is usually clear of snow by mid-June, though spring rain can still leave the mossy rock and roots slick.

April.reason: Snow and ice linger near the Kamikaze ridge crest and on the rock steps, and the steep boot track is wet and slick with snowmelt.

August.reason: The rock is dry, but the southwest-facing slope bakes in afternoon heat, the tread turns loose and dusty, and there is no water above the falls.

October.reason: Autumn rain wets the moss and roots again, and the seasonal trailhead gate closes earlier as the days shorten.

November.reason: Rain-soaked rock and the first snow near the crest make the steep boot track treacherous, especially on descent.

September.reason: Cooler temperatures on the exposed slope and dry rock steps before the autumn rains return.

before.approach: Follow the Mount Teneriffe Trail from the paved trailhead on SE Mount Si Road to the signed Teneriffe Falls junction at about 0.9 mile, turn right, and follow the Teneriffe Falls Trail to the falls viewpoint at about 2.8 miles. From just below the viewpoint, the unofficial but well-traveled Kamikaze Trail boot track climbs directly up the forested southwest ridge/flank of the mountain, gaining about 2,300 ft in roughly one mile of steep, rocky, single-track tread before reaching the Kamikaze Ridge crest (~3,900 ft) and continuing to a cedar-grove shelf (~4,200 ft) that meets the upper mountain near the summit.

pro_tips: Arrive early on weekends — the paved ~70-car lot fills by mid-morning in summer.
The final push to the summit is a short but genuine rock scramble; take it slowly if the rock is wet.
Consider descending via the Kamikaze Trail (or vice versa) to make a scenic ~10-mile loop instead of an out-and-back.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July to September, when the ridge crest, the flat below Green Mountain and the summit scramble are all snow-free

May.reason: Lingering snow on the ridge crest and the flat below Green Mountain creates steep, icy sections on an otherwise Class 1-2 trail.

July.reason: The whole trail and the brief Class 2 summit finish are snow-free, with long days well inside the trailhead gate hours.

June.reason: The last snow near the ridge crest usually melts out during the month, leaving only short patches below the summit scramble.

April.reason: The old logging-road grade melts out, but snow persists above about 3,500 ft and on the ridge crest, turning the upper trail into a snow slog.

March.reason: The trailhead is open, but the upper switchbacks, Rachor Pass and the summit rocks hold steep, icy snow that needs traction and an axe.

August.reason: Dry trail and summit rocks; carry all your water, since there is none above Teneriffe Falls on the hot upper switchbacks.

October.reason: Still usually snow-free, but the rain returns and the seasonal gate closes earlier as the days shorten.

November.reason: The first snow returns to the summit and ridge crest, and the short days leave little time before the trailhead gate closes.

September.reason: Snow-free and cooler than midsummer, with clear views from the summit before the autumn rains set in.

before.approach: From I-90 take Exit 31 into North Bend and continue on North Bend Way; turn left (north) on SE Mount Si Road. Continue about 2.9 miles, past the Little Si and Mount Si trailheads, to the paved, ~70-car Mount Teneriffe Trailhead lot (Discover Pass required). From the lot, a half-mile access path switchbacks up through second-growth forest to an old logging-road grade, which climbs gently for about 1.5 miles through young forest and meadow, passing the signed spur to Teneriffe Falls at about 0.9 mile. Beyond the road grade the trail narrows and climbs via switchbacks (with a Middle Fork Snoqualmie viewpoint) for another ~2.7 miles, then continues about 2.3 more miles, dipping briefly to Rachor Pass (~4,200 ft saddle) before the final short, rocky summit scramble.

what_to_bring: helmet — essential given the loose rock throughout
watch_out: The route 'specializes in loose' rock — helmet mandatory
The approach gully is steep and hideously chossy
A wedged chockstone near the notch may require care to pass
pro_tips: Earlier-season snow in the approach gully can make for a faster, easier ascent than a fully snow-free late-season gully
Existing sling anchors at the notch speed up the return

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, when snow still fills the loose notch gully but Crescent Creek Basin and the climber's track have melted out

May.reason: Deep snow covers the steep Terror Creek climber's track and Crescent Creek Basin, and the gully to the notch is an avalanche path.

July.reason: Firm snow still covers much of the loose gully while the basin opens up, though undercut snow and a moat may force moves along the edge.

June.reason: Snow fills the choss gully and smooths the approach, but the basin can be fully snow-covered and the gully slopes stay avalanche-prone.

August.reason: The gully melts out to loose rock and the chockstone near the notch, raising rockfall risk and requiring the low-5th crack moves.

October.reason: Early snow over loose rock in the gully and on the ridge, and the Marblemount permit office cuts its hours in mid-October.

September.reason: The fully snow-free gully is a loose rubble chute, cold nights ice the notch crack, and shorter days lengthen a long day from camp.

before.approach: From the Hoh River Trailhead (end of Upper Hoh Road, roughly 18 miles east of US-101 south of Forks), follow the Hoh River Trail upriver — a well-graded, mostly flat rainforest path through old-growth Sitka spruce and big-leaf maple for its first ~12 miles. Checkpoints: Mount Tom Creek camp (~mile 2.5-3, elev ~600-700 ft), the first spot with real views of Mount Tom's icefields across the valley; 5 Mile Island (mile 5); Happy Four shelter camp (mile 5.8); Olympus Guard Station (mile 9, water plus a ranger kiosk, with the High Divide/Bogachiel Peak junction 0.6 mile beyond); Lewis Meadow (mile 10.3); and Elk Lake (mile 14.8, elev ~2,500 ft), the last reliable camp and a common high-camp/turnaround point. Past Elk Lake the trail steepens hard, gaining roughly 1,800 ft in the final 2.3 miles to Glacier Meadows (mile 17.1-17.6, elev ~4,200-4,300 ft), the standard high camp for both Mount Olympus and Mount Tom objectives. About half a mile below Glacier Meadows a major washout forces a fixed-ladder descent/crossing (roughly 100 ft, rope-assisted, one person on the ladder at a time) — treat this as the approach trail's own crux hazard, not just a nuisance. From Glacier Meadows, take the Lateral Moraine Trail (~0.8 mile, +800 ft) up onto the moraine crest for the first full view of the Blue Glacier and the terrain beyond; a shorter Terminal Moraine Trail (0.4 mile) offers an alternate viewpoint. From the moraine, glacier travel begins: descend onto and cross the (crevassed) Blue Glacier roped as a team, then climb the broad snow dome (Snow Dome) that most Olympus parties also ascend. Rather than continuing toward Olympus's summit, the Mount Tom line splits off Snow Dome and traverses horizontally along the snowy upper massif, staying below the main Olympus peaks, until it connects with Mount Tom's own White Glacier (on its NE slope) or drops via the Hubert Glacier on the south side to reach the Mount Tom-Olympus connecting ridge. Expect open crevasses on both the Blue and White/Hubert Glaciers requiring standard roped glacier travel, and a final class 3-4 scramble over loose rock to the summit block. Water is abundant along the Hoh River Trail itself (river and creek crossings throughout) but is glacier-melt/snowmelt only above Glacier Meadows, so plan treatment accordingly. The round-trip distance (~69 km/43 mi) reflects the long valley approach plus the extended high-massif traverse to Tom and back — well beyond a standard Olympus summit day. An alternate approach comes from the Bailey Range side: follow the Sol Duc River/High Divide trail system to Cat Basin, then the off-trail Bailey Range crest (over Stephen Peak, Mount Pulitzer, Mount Fitzhenry, and Ferry Basin) to reach the Mount Tom-Olympus col area, rather than via the Hoh River/Blue Glacier.

pro_tips: The first two leads on the north rib are solid, exposed class-5.5 rock — quality drops higher on the route
Budget a full day: 6-8 hours up and roughly 5 hours down is typical from the base
before.descent_text: Reported round-trip climbing time is roughly 6-8 hours up and about 5 hours down from the base, on loose terrain that demands careful downclimbing/rappelling through the brushy, broken lower rib.
